status.reason: Single study no longer fits: the claim rests on several independent trials (head-to-head trials from Thailand, Iran and China; placebo-controlled trials from Malaysia and China; a usual-care trial from Hong Kong). Replicated does not fit either, because no comparison has been tested twice with a consistent, checkable direction. The only pair tested twice, aripiprazole vs risperidone, has Wang 2016 with no between-group difference (p = 0.73, Hall Table 2) and Farnia 2014 with p < 0.001 on SAPS (0.08 on SANS), whose direction the reviews give both ways: Hall's text favours aripiprazole while its footnoted change values favour risperidone; Fluyau's text favours risperidone while its Table 3 says the reverse. The two placebo-controlled trials agree in direction but are known only through reviews that give the aripiprazole trial's result as p < 0.005, p < 0.05 or p = 0.032, and the paliperidone trial's printed means fall by similar amounts (3.8 and 3.3 points) beside p = 0.006 from a Cox model. Mixed fits, but for the reason §6.4 gives, inconsistent findings without an adequate explanation: the aripiprazole–risperidone pair; paliperidone favoured over placebo after the acute phase (Wang 2019) but not over usual care on CGI-S (Chung: p = 0.09 at 12 months, 0.94 at 24); global ratings against symptom ratings within the usual-care trial. Differences in comparator, dose and duration are plausible explanations, but none has been tested. Reader 19's stated reason (populations, outcomes and risk of bias differ) describes indirectness and risk of bias, not inconsistency, and should be replaced. Fairness to Chung 2026: the wording is fair. The registry history bears it out. The primary outcome, relapse at 36 months, was unchanged from 2018 to version 13 (4 July 2025) and was replaced in version 14 (12 November 2025, BPRS-24) and version 15 (23 March 2026, CGI), after actual primary completion (31 May 2024) and actual study completion (31 May 2025). The follow-up was not cut from 36 to 24 months before then: every registered time frame changed from 36 to 24 months in the same version 14, so the change cannot be read as following an earlier change of design. Two precise touches would help: the registry names schizophrenia, not schizoaffective disorder, among its exclusions; and the 36-month time frames were shortened in the same update. Optionally, the article does not mention the change.

grade.reason: Very low is reached on any reasonable reading. (1) A status of mixed (inconsistent findings, no adequate explanation) sits uneasily with 'inconsistency not downgraded'. Either rate inconsistency down one level (the overall does not change) or say why the label and the domain differ. (2) Risk of bias could fairly be −2. The only trial read in full is at high risk (RoB 2): its primary outcome was changed after the trial ended, 30% and 46% of assessments are missing, and the second year was rated unblinded. The two placebo-controlled trials are known only through reviews whose descriptions of their analyses conflict. The reasoning already concedes −2 for the usual-care comparison; the overall does not change. Indirectness −1 and imprecision −2 are right as written.

plain.reason: It says no more than the statement or the sources. Eight short trials in three reviews, about 500 people (514, Hall). Six compared one medicine with another and found no clear winner. Two placebo trials in people already improving (Wang 2019: stabilised before discharge; Sulaiman 2013: per the network meta-analysis) and one two-year trial against usual care favoured the medicine on some measures, with serious flaws. No study of stopping (Hall: none followed people after antipsychotics were stopped). 'Meth psychosis' simplifies, since two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis and about one in ten in the usual-care trial had never used methamphetamine; that is acceptable in plain text.

plain.proposed: Across 27 studies of meth-related psychosis, mostly in hospital patients, the typical study found 1 in 4 people still had symptoms over a month after stopping; studies ranged from none to almost all. Later diagnoses of schizophrenia varied from about 1 in 20 to about 2 in 5 between studies; a 2020 review that averaged five very different studies of amphetamine-type psychosis found about 1 in 5. This does not show meth caused it. Psychosis often returns with renewed use.
